title: OCC Guides Bank Examiners to Assess AI Risk Within Existing Categories
excerpt: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) issued Bulletin 2026-54 Wednesday, Nov. 4, with an examiner framework directing bank examiners to assess artificial intelligence (AI) within existing risk categories and tailor reviews to each system’s use and potential consequences. It covers routine bank activity from credit decisions and payments to fraud detection, customer service, operations, risk management and market activity. Discover more. Banks. Open Bank Account. bank. The framework uses “super intelligence” (SI) for technologies within the existing statutory definition of AI. It places SI within established supervisory categories rather than treating it as its own category. “Examiners should not treat SI as a separate and distinct risk category,” the OCC said in Bulletin 2026-54. Banks do not need to set a separate risk appetite for SI. The guide is an examiner resource that creates no new supervisory expectations or bank requirements. It is not intended as a self-assessment tool for banks’ SI use or risk management. Examiners may also use the framework for community banks, tailoring reviews to each bank’s size, complexity and risk profile. The framework contains 16 components grouped into six pillars and an illustrative scale with four risk tiers. A fully autonomous payment agent that interacts with customers is an example of Tier 1. An internal productivity tool with no exposure to customer or financial data is an example of Tier 4; the tiers are illustrative, not required bank classifications. Risk reviews are guided by a use case’s materiality, its potential consequences, the authority transferred to a system and the degree of human oversight, rather than technical sophistication alone. For uses with greater potential impact, examiners may look for narrower system authority, closer human involvement, added controls, independent testing and operational safeguards. The framework supplements existing model-risk, governance, technology, compliance and operational-risk practices, where SI use can introduce, amplify or modify risks such as operational, compliance and credit risk. The April 17, 2026, interagency model-risk update excluded generative and agentic AI models. The OCC framework is more applicable to those uses, while the April guidance remains relevant to non-generative, non-agentic models. The OCC plans to update the examiner guide as the technology, its uses and supervisory understanding change. Discover more. Learn AI Tools. banks. Bank. Riza Dagoc. title: What AI agents can do for banks' customer relationships
excerpt: Artificial Intelligence. What AI agents can do for banks' customer relationships. By Melinda Lucy. About Melinda. mailto. melinda. lucy@americanbanker. com. linkedin. melinda-huspen. Published November 06, 2026, 7:00 a. m. EST. |. Updated November 06, 2026, 7:01 a. m. EST. 3 Min Read. Facebook. Twitter. LinkedIn. Email. Key insight: Some banks are using AI to improve their relationships with small businesses. Expert quote: "We're not looking for it to go out and contact our customers, because that is the core of who we say we are. We're looking for ways that we can utilize it in-house that will create efficiencies so that we can do a better job of being in front of our customer. "—Cristin Reid, CEO of Capitol National Bank. The next wave of artificial intelligence offers promises of autonomous agents for banks to deploy across different departments. For small business-focused banks, agentic AI is presenting both challenges and opportunities for relationship managers as they work to serve their business clients better. "Many of the opportunities lie around the democratization and the accessibility of data that AI creates," Michael Desimone, chief banking and lending officer at Citadel Federal Credit Union, said during a panel at American Banker's Small Business Banking conference last week. "It's all out there for us, but it's sort of unmanageable and hard to get your arms around. The ability to not spend hours pouring over research and memos to have a good, solid understanding of what a business needs, what it does and where it fits in its segment is very valuable. ". Processing Content. The raw internal data a bank typically has at its disposal often needs to be identified, sorted and curated to determine what is relevant, according to Gary Class, global industry strategist for analytics firm Teradata. Both the company and its bank customers have been using agentic AI to improve the efficiency of data clean-up, he said. "That can be a very painful process, and that's one thing where agentic AI has really come to the fore," he said. Capitol National Bank CEO Cristin Reid said that small banks, such as Capitol, aren't necessarily looking for AI agents to take the place of interpersonal relationship building. "We're not looking for it to go out and contact our customers, because that is the core of who we say we are," she said. "We're looking for ways that we can utilize it in-house that will create efficiencies so that we can do a better job of being in front of our customer. ". Reid explained that Capitol is currently bringing agentic AI to back-office operations such as BSA and AML detection, and is developing a deposit attrition model that can flag at-risk customers to relationship managers. "It will integrate our core system and pull information about each one of our customers and their deposit activity," she said. "Are their transactions staying the same? Did they change their address? Did they stop a recurring deposit that's going in? What are the key indicators that could hint to us that they're considering going to another bank or moving? It will rank those customers based on risk, then it talks directly to the CRM model. That's going to put the emphasis for us on maintaining that relationship. ". Desimone noted that bank regulations need to rapidly evolve around agentic AI models. "If you think back over places where regulators have had to adapt, it's usually after some kind of a crisis or when something material goes awry," he said. "There's been small instances of that but no major ones yet. We're going to learn on the fly, and someone will be the sacrificial organization that we all learn from because things don't go well for them. That's harsh, but it's reality. ". Reid emphasized that banks can also build their internal governance models with AI in mind from the outset. FINANCE. 05-11-2026 14:40 HKT. by. Zhou Yiru. From left: Song Jianing; Vivian Khoo, chief executive and managing director of PWMA. Private banking and wealth management assets in Hong Kong surged 24 percent to a record HK$12. 9 trillion in 2025, amid strong net fund inflows and surging demand for asset booking, according to an industry survey released on Thursday. The Hong Kong Private Wealth Management Report 2026, co-authored by the Private Wealth Management Association (PWMA) and KPMG China, polled executives from 35 private wealth institutions and 17 asset management firms between June and August 2026. The data points to Hong Kong’s resilience as a cross-boundary wealth hub, with net fund inflows jumping 79 percent year-on-year, and 77 percent of surveyed firms reported increased demand for new accounts and asset booking, up from 59 percent a year earlier. None of the respondents reported a decline. Some 94 percent of wealth management firms remain moderately or highly optimistic about the local market’s prospects over the next five years, despite geopolitical uncertainties. Deepening regional ties. Industry players view Greater Bay Area integration and the Wealth Management Connect scheme as important to future growth. According to the report, 79 percent of respondents identified Greater Bay Area initiatives as important to their offshore business over the next five years. Clients continue to view Hong Kong as a trusted platform for managing wealth amidst geopolitical shifts, underscoring the need for the sector to remain competitive and connected, said Amy Lo Choi-wan, chairman of the PWMA executive committee and UBS Hong Kong head and chief executive. Rapid shift toward AI and digital assets. Driven by the need to capture next-generation wealth, 88 percent of firms reported moderate or significant progress in adopting artificial intelligence, generative AI, or agentic AI technologies, a sharp increase from 56 percent in the previous year. KPMG China noted the next phase of value creation will depend on integrating data and re-engineering workflows. Relationship managers still spend roughly 38 percent of their time on routine administrative activities, said Song Jianing, head of banking and capital markets, Hong Kong, at KPMG China. He noted this highlights a critical need for the industry to leverage AI to free up capacity for direct client engagement. Meanwhile, the proportion of firms actively developing digital asset trading platforms, custody services, or product ranges increased from 16 percent to 25 percent over the past year. An additional 13 percent of firms already offer such services, while 43 percent have added cryptocurrency exchange-traded funds or products to their offerings. wealth management private banking PWMA. Bei der jüngsten Ausgabe der Next Leaders-Reihe der BW-Bank im Stuttgarter Restaurant Feinkost Böhm kamen Unternehmens- und Vermögensnachfolger bei einem exklusiven Dinner zusammen, um sich mit der Zukunft des Unternehmertums im Zeitalter künstlicher Intelligenz auseinanderzusetzen. LBBW-Innovationschef Stephan Paxmann zeigte im Gespräch mit Forbes, warum jahrzehntelanger Erfolg keine Garantie für die Zukunft ist – und welche Verantwortung die nächste Generation bei der Fortführung von Unternehmen und Vermögen trägt, insbesondere wenn es darum geht, bestehende Geschäftsmodelle grundlegend neu zu denken. Ein Unternehmen oder Familienvermögen zu übernehmen bedeutet, auf dem Erfolg früherer Generationen aufzubauen und zugleich wirtschaftliche und gesellschaftliche Verantwortung zu tragen. Doch künstliche Intelligenz (KI) verändert die Spielregeln gerade nachhaltig: Geschäftsmodelle, die über Jahrzehnte erfolgreich waren, geraten unter Druck und Unternehmer müssen sich neu aufstellen. Genau um dieses Spannungsfeld zwischen unternehmerischem Erbe und technologischem Wandel ging es am 2. November 2026 bei der BW-Bank X Next Leaders-Reihe in Stuttgart. Im Mittelpunkt stand die Frage, wie sich Unternehmen auf eine Zukunft vorbereiten können, in der KI nicht nur einzelne Arbeitsprozesse verändert, sondern ganze Branchen neu ordnet. Silke Siegel-Kirschenmann, Leiterin Wealth Management Stuttgart bei der BW-Bank, betonte in ihrer Begrüßung die hohe wirtschaftliche und gesellschaftliche Verantwortung, die mit der Übernahme von Unternehmen oder Familienvermögen einhergeht. «Wir wollen Sie begleiten und Ihnen das richtige Werkzeug an die Hand geben», erklärte sie. Genau hier setzt die Next Leaders-Reihe an: Sie bringt die nächste Generation von Unternehmens- und Vermögensnachfolgern zusammen, fördert den Austausch unter Gleichgesinnten und bietet Impulse für die Herausforderungen, die mit der Verantwortung für Unternehmen, Vermögen und deren Rolle in der Gesellschaft einhergehen. KI: zwischen Dystopie und Utopie Wie tiefgreifend KI die Wirtschaft verändern wird, diskutierte Stephan Paxmann, Chief Innovation Officer der Landesbank Baden-Württemberg (LBBW), mit Andrea Gläsemann, stellvertretende Chefredakteurin von Forbes Swiss. Paxmann, der selbst ein Unternehmen gegründet und zwölf Jahre als Vorstandsvorsitzender geführt hatte, ordnete die aktuelle KI-Debatte zwischen dystopischen Zukunftsszenarien und technologischen Heilsversprechen ein. «Die Geschäftsmodelle sind at risk, aber nicht die Technologie», so Paxmann und führte weiter aus: «Wir können noch viel, viel mehr von KI erwarten. ». Deutschlands Ausgangslage im internationalen Vergleich bewertete Paxmann hierbei optimistischer, als es die öffentliche Debatte vermuten lässt. «Wir dürfen uns nicht schlechter machen, als wir sind. » An technologischer Kompetenz, industriellem Know-how und Innovationskraft mangelt es aus seiner Sicht nicht. Die Schwäche liegt für ihn vielmehr darin, aus guten Ideen profitable Geschäftsmodelle zu entwickeln. Während die USA und asiatische Länder Innovationen schneller kommerzialisieren, sieht er Deutschland durch Risikoaversion und regulatorische Hürden gebremst. Sein Appell: «Man wird nicht für Sicherheit bezahlt, sondern für Risiko. ». «AI First» beginnt in der Chefetage Jahrzehnte erfolgreicher Unternehmensgeschichte schützen nicht davor, dass neue Wettbewerber bestehende Geschäftsmodelle mithilfe von KI schneller und kostengünstiger reproduzieren. Paxmanns Antwort ist das Prinzip «AI First»: Künstliche Intelligenz soll von Anfang an in unternehmerische Überlegungen und Entscheidungen einbezogen werden. Nicht alles muss KI übernehmen. Doch bei jeder Aufgabe sollte zunächst geprüft werden, ob die Technologie eine bessere oder effizientere Lösung ermöglicht. Das allein reicht jedoch nicht aus. title: Aké Festival And Sterling Bank: When African Wisdom Meets Artificial Intelligence
excerpt: Travel. Aké Festival And Sterling Bank: When African Wisdom Meets Artificial Intelligence. by Apata Oyeniran November 6, 2026. written by Apata Oyeniran November 6, 2026. Share 0 Facebook Twitter Pinterest Email. A grand cultural. perfirmance during the 2026 Omo Olowo day in Abeokuta, Ogun State. 0 Sterling Bank has renewed its partnership with the Aké Arts and Book Festival, one of Africa’s foremost gatherings of writers, artists and thinkers, as the festival returns to Lagos from 19 to 21 November 2026 with a conversation about Africa’s place in an increasingly technology-driven world. Now in its 14th edition, the festival will explore the theme ‘Native Intelligence’, examining the relationship between the knowledge Africans have developed and passed down for generations and the artificial intelligence systems increasingly influencing how people live, learn, work and communicate. The theme stems from a simple fact: Africa was thinking long before machines were. The elders, the proverb and the folktale represent systems of knowledge refined over centuries. Today, artificial intelligence is changing how stories are told, how elections are fought and how truth is reported worldwide. Yet questions remain about how adequately African languages, experiences and cultural contexts are represented in the technologies increasingly shaping the world. For Sterling Bank, which has supported the festival since 2018, the partnership represents a continued investment in the people and ideas shaping Africa’s cultural and intellectual future. Over the years, Aké has provided a meeting point for established and emerging writers, artists and thinkers, bringing together more than 1,000 creative voices and creating opportunities for African stories and perspectives to reach wider audiences. Commenting on this year’s convening, Donatus Okpako, Chief Marketing Officer at Sterling Bank, stated, “Every society has an intelligence, the instinct and judgement employed to read a situation and solve a problem. Africans have always had it in abundance. As AI reshapes how we work, bank, vote and learn, the real concern is whether Africa has its own ways of thinking to help shape the technology it relies on. For fourteen years, Aké has placed African ideas at the centre of global conversations. That is a platform worth standing behind. ”. ‘Native Intelligence’ does not treat African knowledge as a relic to be kept behind glass. It treats it as a living intelligence with a claim on the future. Over three days, novelists, poets, journalists, technologists, filmmakers and scholars will examine who decides what counts as knowledge. They will also ask the question at the heart of the festival: whose intelligence are we building the future on?. Lola Shoneyin, Founder and Director of the Aké Arts and Book Festival, said, “A machine knows only what it has been fed, and it has not been fed much of us. Native Intelligence is about power: who decides what is true, what is worth remembering, and whose voice the future speaks in? Sterling understands our goal to support and celebrate creativity on the African continent and beyond. We are delighted to work with them again. ”. You Might Be Interested In.
